idiom_name: Warden strategies (Warden::Strategies.add) cascaded by label; Devise on top
implementation_notes: Warden is the seam beneath most Ruby web authentication: a strategy is a block or subclass of Warden::Strategies::Base with an optional valid? guard and a required authenticate! that ends in success!(user) or fail!(message), registered under a label via Warden::Strategies.add; env['warden'].authenticate(:password, :basic) cascades strategies until one succeeds, halts or fails, and the resulting user is the principal. Rack's own primitives (Rack::Auth::Basic) are the low-level fallback for a single mechanism. The class hierarchy of the classic pattern is not written by hand.
code_sketch:
Warden::Strategies.add(:password) do
  def valid?
    params['username'] || params['password']
  end

  def authenticate!
    user = User.authenticate(params['username'], params['password'])
    user ? success!(user) : fail!('invalid credentials')
  end
end

env['warden'].authenticate(:password, :basic)   # cascade until one strategy halts
pitfalls: fail! halts the cascade, so a strategy that fails on the wrong credential shape prevents later strategies from running - guard it with valid?.
success!/fail! must be reached exactly once per authenticate! call; forgetting the success path silently leaves the request unauthenticated.
Storing the full user (or its password digest) in the session is a data leak; serialize an identifier and reload.
Devise modules (lockable, timeoutable, trackable) change authentication semantics through configuration; audit them instead of assuming defaults.
